questions.passage: Horses and toads can see in three dimensions (3D), which helps them perceive distance and depth. Octopuses and squid are thought to lack 3D vision. Many researchers once thought the same about cuttlefish, but Trevor Wardill and his team wanted to test whether this assumption was true. The team studied how cuttlefish wearing 3D glasses reacted to 3D images of shrimp (a favorite prey) projected on a tank wall. Cuttlefish changed their striking position to match the 3D images, suggesting that their vision is more like that of horses and toads than that of octopuses or squid.
questions.prompt: Which choice best states the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It explains how 3D vision in horses and toads differs from the type of 3D vision discussed in the text.
choices.B: It offers a suggestion for future research on the aspect of 3D vision discussed in the text.
choices.C: It presents the results of the study of 3D vision discussed in the text.
choices.D: It explains why the animals discussed in the text were once thought to lack 3D vision.

questions.passage: Boston has high pedestrian traffic, but simply replicating a feature of Boston associated with walkability —e.g., its high number of intersections—may be insufficient to induce increased walking in other cities. As urbanist Mariela Alfonzo argues, our understanding of individuals’ decision-making about whether to walk is insufficiently robust: some studies emphasize the role of population density, others the role of individual physical fitness, and so on, but walking decisions are made in complex contexts in which multiple conditions and needs inform individuals’ choices.
questions.prompt: Which choice best describes the function of the references to “population density” and “individual physical fitness” in the text as a whole?

choices.A: They represent factors that have been identified as important influences on walking decisions but that the text suggests are merely some of the many factors that may contribute to people’s decision-making about walking.
choices.B: They are examples of factors that studies suggest are important in people’s decision making about walking but that the text claims most people rarely consider when making walking decisions.
choices.C: They identify factors that Alfonzo argues have been overemphasized in studies of decision- making about walking but that the text asserts are relevant to most people’s walking decisions.
choices.D: They illustrate factors that researchers believe people consider when making walking decisions in most contexts but that the text argues are unique to walking decisions made by people in Boston.

questions.passage: Fish whose DNA has been modified to include genetic material from other species are known as transgenic. Some transgenic fish have genes from jellyfish that result in fluorescence (that is, they glow in the dark). Although these fish were initially engineered for research purposes in the 1990s, they were sold as pets in the 2000s and can now be found in the wild in creeks in Brazil. A student in a biology seminar who is writing a paper on these fish asserts that their escape from Brazilian fish farms into the wild may have significant negative long-term ecological effects.
questions.prompt: Which quotation from a researcher would best support the student’s assertion?

choices.A: “In one site in the wild where transgenic fish were observed, females outnumbered males, while in another the numbers of females and males were equivalent.”
choices.B: “Though some presence of transgenic fish in the wild has been recorded, there are insufficient studies of the impact of those fish on the ecosystems into which they are introduced.”
choices.C: “The ecosystems into which transgenic fish are known to have been introduced may represent a subset of the ecosystems into which the fish have actually been introduced.”
choices.D: “Through interbreeding, transgenic fish might introduce the trait of fluorescence into wild fish populations, making those populations more vulnerable to predators.”

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

choices.C: The traditional approach to dyeing blue jeans is to dip them in a solution containing hazardous chemicals.
choices.D: Rai’s approach substitutes a natural plant-based substance for the hazardous chemicals that manufacturers have traditionally used.

P waves compress and expand the ground, causing it to move backward and forward. S waves cause the ground to move from side to side.

choices.D: Although P waves and S waves start at the same point, they behave very differently.

questions.passage:
Text 1
In separate studies, Yanbo Xiao and colleagues and Sana Wahbi and colleagues examined whether plants transfer nutrients to one another using a common mycorrhizal network (CMN) a lattice of fungal strands in the soil.
